_comment: Golden vectors for the capability report (T3.5). These hex strings were
derived by hand from RFC 8949 §3 and the key assignment in capability.h —
not produced by running the encoder. That is the entire point of the file.
A round-trip test proves the two ends of one implementation agree with each
other; it says nothing about whether the bytes on the wire are the bytes
the protocol specifies. Regenerating these from the code would turn the
check into a tautology, so: never regenerate. If a vector fails, the
encoder changed, and that is a protocol change requiring a version bump.

why_positional: A map per component would cost five key bytes each — forty bytes over
eight components against a hundred-byte budget — to describe a shape the
protocol fixes and which could not be reordered anyway.

cases.name: empty report
cases.derivation: A3 map(3) | 01 key | 01 fw=1 | 02 key | 00 heap=0 | 03 key | 80 array(0)

cases.name: a BME680 and a GPIO, as a real node reports them
derivation: 01 key | 1A 00040000  fw=262144 needs the 4-byte argument form
02 key | 18 C0        heap=192 is above 23, so one extra byte
85 array(5) | 10 type=16 | 18 76 addr=0x76 above 23 | 00 i2c | 04 ch | 01 configured
85 array(5) | 11 type=17 | 04 pin 4 | 01 gpio | 02 ch | 00 flags

cases.name: every field sitting on the 23/24 argument-width seam
derivation: The boundary that matters for canonical encoding: 23 is carried in the
initial byte, 24 needs a following byte. Two encoders that disagree
here produce different wire bytes for the same report and still pass
every round-trip test either of them runs alone.
A3 | 01 17 fw=23 inline | 02 1818 heap=24 spills | 03 81 array(1)
